article.title: Why Carriers Fail: From Shared Support to Structural Misfit
article.summary: Carrier failure is rarely a sudden disappearance. Capacity, connection, responsibility, and replacement paths can drift out of fit; what ultimately matters is whether important reality can still be carried forward.

blocks.text: Carrier failure is rarely a sudden disappearance. Capacity, connection, responsibility, and replacement paths can drift out of fit; what ultimately matters is whether important reality can still be carried forward.

The easiest mistake in reading a carrier is to treat “still present” as “still able to carry.” A body can still function, a relationship can still retain its form, an organization can still exist on paper, and a system can still start up without being able to carry the same reality it once did. Carrying is a relationship: the carrier still needs enough capacity, resources, connection, and authority for reality to enter, run, and complete through it.

Failure therefore often begins in partial functions. Some responsibilities become harder to hold, some interfaces interrupt repeatedly, and things that once completed naturally require increasing compensation. Because the carrier has not stopped entirely, reality keeps assigning old responsibilities to it: people add attention, relationships add explanation, organizations add coordination, and systems add manual checks. Compensation can delay interruption while hiding the fact that carrying conditions have changed.

Mature maintenance must separate two goals: preserving the original carrier and preserving continuity of what the carrier was meant to hold. Sometimes the goals align; sometimes they do not. If recovery or repair can return the carrier to a reasonable range, protecting it makes sense. If the carrying relationship can no longer continue, functions, data, responsibilities, knowledge, or relationships may need to migrate, reorganize, or be replaced, and some operations may need to end.

This is why alternative paths and redundancy are not automatically waste. When critical knowledge exists in one person, every decision passes through one interface, or all data depends on one location, apparent efficiency concentrates continuity in a single point of failure. Durable operation needs to know in advance how knowledge can be handed over, responsibility transferred, data migrated, and authority lawfully continued.

Different carriers fail in different ways. Living carriers change with physical condition, environment, and life stage, so past output cannot be treated as a permanent standard. Persistent functional decline, recurring symptoms, or meaningful risk should bring appropriate medical or other professional judgment into the picture; a runtime model cannot diagnose them. Relationship carriers depend on enough trust, boundaries, responsibility, and communication for shared operation to continue.

Organizations and collectives depend more heavily on transferable knowledge, rules, responsibilities, and shared reference points. If an organization loses core function as soon as a key person leaves, part of what looked like organizational capability was actually personal capability being temporarily borrowed. If members remain but no longer trust shared rules or cannot use shared resources together, what has weakened is the connective capacity of the shared reality.

So the central question in carrier failure is not whether the thing still exists. It is whether the critical connections still work: between body and reality, member and member, responsibility and resources, rules and actual behavior. Repair what can be repaired, transfer what must move, and allow what should end to end. Continuity does not require an eternal carrier; it requires important reality to be carryable again when carriers change.

blocks.label: Key judgment
blocks.text: A carrier can still exist after the carrying relationship has failed; maintenance ultimately protects continuity of reality, not the permanence of the original carrier.

blocks.label: Reality Question
blocks.text: What are you trying to preserve now: a structure that can still carry the reality it serves, or an old position that already needs migration, reorganization, or an ending?
